common_name: Matsunami Azalea (Old White Red-Striped Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Matsunami is among the oldest recorded Satsuki cultivars, grown continuously in Japan since the late 17th century.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Matsunami is a historic Satsuki azalea, among the oldest named cultivars still grown, bearing relatively small white flowers irregularly striped and flecked with red late in the Satsuki bloom season. Its habit is densely multi-branched with slightly rounded leaves, and growth is slow but sturdy, making it a long-favored subject for bonsai as well as container and border planting. As with other Satsuki selections, prune only right after flowering, since next year's buds form soon after bloom ends.

common_name: Asuka Azalea (White Purple-Edged Large-Flowered Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Asuka is a modern registered Satsuki hybrid grown mainly by collectors and bonsai enthusiasts.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Asuka is a late 20th-century Satsuki hybrid bearing large white flowers edged and flushed with purple, a striking bicolor pattern among the larger-flowered Satsuki selections. Its habit and culture otherwise follow typical Satsuki azalea care: slow, dense growth suited to container culture and bonsai training, with flowering later in spring than Kurume or Southern Indica types. Water deeply in dry weather and shear or prune only in the brief window right after bloom.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Hakatajiro is one of the old historic Satsuki cultivars, prized for dependable white flowers and good winter hardiness.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching well to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Hakatajiro is a historic, slow-growing Satsuki cultivar valued for its clean white flowers and compact, densely twiggy habit, which have made it a long-standing parent in Satsuki breeding as well as a popular subject for shohin (small) bonsai. It tolerates somewhat cooler winters better than many Satsuki selections. As with other Satsuki, prune or pinch only right after flowering, since buds for the next season form soon after bloom.

common_name: Hi-no-Maru Azalea (White Red-Centered Satsuki Azalea, 'Rising Sun')

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Hi-no-Maru takes its name from Japan's rising-sun flag, which its bloom color pattern is said to resemble.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Hi-no-Maru bears white flowers marked with a solid, well-centered red blotch or throat, a pattern that holds more consistently from bloom to bloom than the heavy sporting typical of many Satsuki cultivars, and the resemblance to Japan's national flag has made it a popular modern variety among Satsuki collectors. Growth and care otherwise follow standard Satsuki culture, with a dense, compact habit suited to container growing and bonsai training. Prune only in the short window right after flowering, since flower buds for the following year form soon afterward.

common_name: Yata-no-Kagami Azalea (Variable Red-and-White Sporting Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Yata-no-Kagami takes its name from the mythical mirror of Japanese legend and is grown for its strongly variable flower pattern.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Yata-no-Kagami is grown for its unusually strong sporting: a single plant can carry solid red flowers, solid white flowers, and red flowers with white centers all in the same season, a trait Satsuki collectors prize for its unpredictability from year to year. Culture matches other Satsuki selections, with slow, dense growth well suited to containers and bonsai training, and later bloom timing than Kurume or Southern Indica azaleas. Prune only right after flowering to avoid removing next year's buds.

common_name: Amagasa Azalea (Vivid Orange-Red Large-Flowered Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Amagasa was widely used by mid-20th-century American azalea hybridizers for its large, vivid flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Amagasa produces notably large, vivid orange-red flowers later in spring than most evergreen azaleas, and its strong color and flower size made it an influential parent for American breeders working with Satsuki stock in the mid-20th century, even though it is grown today more as a landscape shrub than a bonsai subject. Its habit is dense and compact like other Satsuki selections, tolerating the repeated shearing typical of the group. Prune only right after flowering, since buds for the following season form soon after bloom.

common_name: Alexander Clematis Montana (Large Cream-White Spring Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Alexander is a spring-blooming Clematis montana selection that flowers on the previous year's growth and should be pruned only right after flowering, if at all.

directions: Alexander is one of the largest-flowered selections of Clematis montana, bearing four-petaled, cream-white blooms 3 to 4 inches across with prominent golden-yellow stamens, set against pale green foliage. Like other montanas it produces a single overwhelming flush of spring bloom on old wood rather than repeat flowering, and its vigorous habit needs a sturdy, large support such as a fence, arbor, or mature tree. Give it well-drained soil with a cool, shaded root run and full sun to partial shade on the top growth.

common_name: Vera Clematis Montana (Fragrant Pale Pink Spring Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Vera is a spring-blooming Clematis montana selection that flowers on the previous year's growth and should be pruned only right after flowering, if at all.

directions: Vera bears pale pink, four-petaled flowers with greenish-yellow stamens and a strong, sweet fragrance, opening in great profusion in late spring along the previous year's growth. Like other Clematis montana selections it is extremely vigorous, so give it a sturdy, large support and allow it room to ramble over a fence, pergola, or mature tree. Keep the root zone cool, moist, and shaded with mulch or underplanting, with the top growth in full sun to partial shade, and prune only right after flowering if size needs controlling.

common_name: Odorata Clematis Montana (Vanilla-Scented Pink-to-White Spring Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Odorata is a spring-blooming Clematis montana var. rubens selection that flowers on the previous year's growth and should be pruned only right after flowering, if at all.

directions: Odorata opens pale pink and fades to near white as the flowers age, carrying an intense, sweet vanilla scent that is especially strong among montana selections, with the bronze-purple young foliage typical of var. rubens maturing to green. It flowers in a single dense spring flush on the previous year's wood and grows vigorously, so plant it against a sturdy fence, wall, or large arbor with room to spread. Keep the root run cool and shaded while allowing the vine itself full sun to partial shade, and prune only right after bloom if needed.

common_name: Fragrant Spring Clematis Montana (Sweetly Scented Clear Pink Spring Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Fragrant Spring is a vigorous Clematis montana selection that flowers on the previous year's growth and should be pruned only right after flowering, if at all.

directions: Fragrant Spring bears clear pink, single flowers with pale yellow-green stamens in such profusion that the bronze-tinted foliage is largely hidden from late spring into early summer, and the sweet scent carries well beyond the plant itself. It is an especially vigorous montana selection capable of covering 20 to 30 feet of fence, wall, or mature tree in time, so give it a very sturdy support from the start. Keep the root zone cool, moist, and shaded, with the vine itself in full sun to partial shade, and prune only right after flowering since buds form on the prior year's growth.

common_name: Little White Charm Armand Clematis (Compact Fragrant White Evergreen Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Little White Charm (also sold as 'Meyeniana') is a more compact, especially fragrant selection of evergreen Armand clematis that, like the species, blooms very early on the previous year's growth, so prune only right after flowering.

directions: Little White Charm is a more restrained, compact selection of evergreen Armand clematis, smothering its dark, leathery, glossy foliage in masses of smaller but unusually profuse, star-shaped creamy-white flowers in early to mid spring. It is noted among armandii selections for especially strong fragrance. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade against a trellis, arbor, or fence, and prune only right after the early spring bloom finishes, since flower buds form on the prior season's wood and later cuts remove the coming display. Established vines tolerate short dry spells but perform best with regular moisture and a mulched, shaded root run.
